hub_intro_html:
Madera sits at a working crossroads of the San Joaquin Valley. Highway 99 carries the county's almonds, pistachios, raisins, and wine north and south; Highway 145 ties the west-side ranches to the city; and Highway 41 climbs out of the flats toward Coarsegold, Oakhurst, and the southern gate of Yosemite. It is also one of the oldest wine regions in the Central Valley — the Madera AVA has been crushing grapes since long before most of California's better-known appellations existed — and that heritage shows up on its rooftops. Wineries, tank farms, crush pads, barrel storage, bottling lines, food-grade processing plants, and the metal ag buildings that serve them all share one thing: big, low-slope roofs that take a beating from the Valley sun and can't afford to leak on the product below.

Allstate Spray Foam Roofing has served this stretch of the Valley for more than twenty years as a family-owned contractor. Our crews dispatch from our Tulare County shop, roughly sixty minutes south of Madera on CA-99, and we treat Madera, Chowchilla, Oakhurst, and Coarsegold as regular working territory — not a long-distance favor. We hold California license #C-2-1052735, we're BBB Accredited, and we're members of the Spray Polyurethane Foam Alliance, the industry body that sets the standards for how spray polyurethane foam roofing should be specified and installed.

Why does spray foam make so much sense here? Start with the climate. Madera summers routinely push past 100°F, and a dark flat roof can run 60 to 80 degrees hotter than the air above it. SPF is the only roofing system that is also insulation — about R-6.5 per inch — so it cuts the heat load on your building at the same time it seals it. In winter, tule fog parks over the Madera Plains for days at a time, keeping roofs damp and exposing every seam, fastener, and flashing failure on conventional systems. A foam roof has no seams to fail: it's applied as a liquid and cures into one continuous, self-flashed membrane around every vent, curb, skylight, and penetration. Add the abrasive ag dust that settles out of harvest air onto every roof in the county, and the case for a monolithic, renewable surface gets even stronger.

For Madera's wine and food-processing facilities, the value goes past waterproofing. Barrel rooms and case-goods storage want temperature stability; SPF's insulation value flattens the daily rooftop temperature swing that drives cooling costs and stresses refrigeration equipment. Processing plants that run washdown regimes and tight sanitation programs can't tolerate ceiling drips or condensation — closed-cell foam on the roof deck or interior walls controls both. And the county's thousands of metal buildings — shops, barns, equipment sheds, warehouses in the Madera Industrial Park and along Avenue 12 — are ideal SPF candidates, because foam locks down oil-canning panels, encapsulates rusting fastener lines, and stops the condensation that rains off bare metal purlins on foggy mornings.

Everything starts with our free roof assessment. We fly a drone survey of the entire roof, pull core samples where the roof's history is unclear, and put a written bid in your hands within 48 hours — real numbers, not a vague range. New spray foam roofs typically run $4–$8 per square foot depending on thickness, access, and prep; recoating an existing foam or coated roof runs $2–$4 per square foot. Because a foam roof is renewed with a fresh silicone topcoat every 10–20 years instead of being torn off, it's often the last roof a Madera building ever needs — see how long spray foam roofing lasts for the full lifecycle math.

Below you'll find our four core services for the Madera area: new spray foam roofing, silicone roof coatings and recoats, roof repair for foam and flat roofs, and commercial spray foam insulation for metal buildings, warehouses, and cold storage. Whether you manage a winery off Avenue 12, a processing plant near the 99, a shop building in Chowchilla, or a commercial roof up the hill in Oakhurst, the first step is the same: call (559) 739-9519 and get real data on your roof within two days.

spray-foam-roofing.body_html:
Spray Foam Roofing Built for Madera's Working Rooftops

Spray foam roofing in Madera solves the two problems every flat and low-slope roof in the county fights at once: relentless Valley heat and water that finds every seam. Madera County's commercial building stock — wineries and wine-processing plants along the 99 corridor, nut hullers and packing houses, warehouses in the Madera Industrial Park, and thousands of metal ag buildings from the west-side plains to the Coarsegold foothills — runs heavily to big, low-slope roofs. Those roofs bake past 150°F surface temperature in July, sit damp under tule fog for weeks in December and January, and collect a steady film of abrasive ag dust in between. Spray polyurethane foam (SPF) is the one roofing system engineered for exactly that duty cycle: a monolithic, fully adhered membrane with no seams, no fasteners, and built-in insulation of roughly R-6.5 per inch.

Allstate Spray Foam Roofing is a family-owned contractor with more than twenty years in the San Joaquin Valley, California license #C-2-1052735, BBB accreditation, and membership in the Spray Polyurethane Foam Alliance. Our crews dispatch from our Tulare County shop, about sixty minutes south of Madera via CA-99 — close enough that Madera, Chowchilla, Oakhurst, and Coarsegold are routine service territory for us, not an occasional stretch.

What a Spray Foam Roof Actually Is

SPF roofing is applied as a liquid. Two components — an isocyanate and a polyol resin — meet at the spray gun, react in seconds, and expand about thirty times in volume into rigid closed-cell foam that bonds directly to your existing roof deck or membrane. The foam cures into one continuous surface with no laps, no welds, and no fastener penetrations. Because the applicator sprays it in place, the foam self-flashes around every curb, pipe, drain, HVAC stand, and skylight — the exact details where conventional roofs fail first. Over the cured foam we apply an elastomeric topcoat, typically high-solids silicone with embedded granules, which shields the foam from UV and gives the roof its weathering surface.

Three properties matter most for a Madera building. First, the finished roof is seamless — there is simply no joint for wind-driven rain or ponded water to exploit. Second, it is fully adhered across its entire area, so leaks cannot travel laterally under the membrane the way they do under mechanically fastened single-ply. Third, it insulates: closed-cell SPF delivers about R-6.5 per inch, so a two-inch application adds roughly R-13 to the top of your building while it waterproofs it. No other roof system does both jobs in one installation. For the full technical background, see our spray polyurethane foam roofing guide.

Why SPF Fits Madera's Climate Better Than Anything Else

Madera sits in California Climate Zone 13, the hot interior of the San Joaquin Valley. Summer highs top 100°F for weeks at a stretch, and rooftop surface temperatures on dark membranes run far higher. That heat does two expensive things: it pours into the building through the roof assembly, driving cooling loads on everything from tasting rooms to refrigerated storage, and it cycles the roof through brutal daily expansion and contraction that fatigues seams, flashings, and fastener lines. A white silicone-coated SPF roof reflects the majority of that solar load, and the foam beneath blocks what's left — buildings in this climate zone commonly see meaningful drops in summer cooling demand after an SPF installation, which also helps projects pencil against California's Title 24 cool-roof and insulation requirements for roof replacements and new low-slope construction.

Winter brings the opposite problem. Tule fog settles over the Madera Plains and the 99 corridor for days at a time, keeping roof surfaces wet without any actual rainfall. Conventional roofs with aging seams wick that persistent moisture into laps and fastener holes; metal roofs drip condensation from every cold purlin. A seamless foam roof gives fog nothing to work with, and the insulation keeps the interior face of the roof assembly above dew point, which shuts down interior condensation. Between those seasons, harvest fills the air with fine ag dust from the county's almond, pistachio, and grape operations — grit that abrades coatings and clogs drains. SPF's smooth, monolithic surface sheds dust to the drains instead of trapping it in seams and ballast.

Winery and Food-Grade Facilities: Where Foam Earns Its Keep

Madera is one of the oldest wine regions in the Central Valley, and its production facilities are a core part of our work in the county. Wineries are unusually demanding roof customers. Barrel rooms and case-goods warehouses want temperature stability — every degree of rooftop heat that gets into the building is a degree the refrigeration plant has to pull back out, and temperature swing is itself an enemy of wine in storage. Crush pads, tank rooms, and bottling halls run sanitation and washdown programs that make ceiling drips, rust flakes, and condensation unacceptable over product and equipment. And harvest season means the roof has to be dependable precisely when a shutdown is most costly.

SPF answers each of those constraints. The insulation value flattens the daily temperature curve inside barrel and case storage, easing refrigeration duty and smoothing out the swings. The seamless membrane eliminates the drip points that plague seamed roofs over processing areas. On metal-roofed tank rooms and barrel barns, foam applied over the panels stops the morning condensation rain that bare metal produces under fog. And because SPF installs over most existing roofs without tear-off, a winery can reroof between vintages — or even during production, since we can sequence work area by area — without opening the building to the sky. The same logic serves Madera's broader food-processing base: nut hullers and processors, raisin and dried-fruit operations, and cold-chain warehouses all get the same combination of dry, stable, and fast.

Metal Ag Buildings: SPF's Home Turf

Drive any avenue west of the 99 and you'll pass the building type spray foam serves best: the pre-engineered metal building. Shops, equipment barns, hay and commodity storage, well houses, and packing sheds across Madera County share the same weaknesses — fastener lines that back out and weep, panel laps that open as the steel expands and contracts, oil-canning that stresses old sealant, rust creeping along every screw head, and condensation that drips off the underside of cold panels onto equipment, feed, and stored crop.

Foam over a metal roof fixes all of it in one pass. The foam encapsulates every fastener and lap, locks the panels together into one rigid diaphragm, and adds enough stiffness to quiet oil-canning. The insulation keeps the panel's interior face warm enough that fog-season condensation never forms. And the silicone topcoat seals out the moisture that drives rust. For a metal building that's structurally sound but leaking at every screw, SPF is nearly always cheaper than re-skinning the roof — and dramatically better insulated afterward. If you're weighing foam against replacing panels or overlaying single-ply, our spray foam vs TPO comparison walks through how the systems differ on exactly this building type.

Commercial Roofing in Madera: Warehouses, Retail, and the Industrial Park

Madera's commercial footprint is growing. The Madera Industrial Park and the corridors along Avenue 12, Avenue 17, and CA-145 have picked up steady logistics and light-industrial spillover as Fresno's distribution market pushes north up the 99, and the Rio Mesa area continues to develop. Most of that stock — tilt-up warehouses, distribution buildings, retail centers, offices — carries flat or low-slope roofs that are ideal SPF candidates. For commercial roofing in Madera, foam offers building owners a specific business case: installation over the existing roof in most cases (no tear-off, no dumpsters, no exposure), a renewable surface that resets with a recoat instead of a replacement, and an insulation upgrade that shows up on every summer utility bill.

For property managers running multiple buildings, the maintenance profile matters as much as the install. An SPF roof is inspected and touched up on a simple schedule, and small damage is repairable with caulk-grade sealant or spot foam by any competent maintenance tech — no heat welders, no proprietary crews for minor work. When the topcoat weathers thin after 10–20 years, a recoat at $2–$4 per square foot renews the roof without touching the foam. That cycle repeats indefinitely, which is why foam roofs from the 1980s are still in service across the Valley.

What a Spray Foam Roof Costs in Madera

New SPF roofing typically runs $4–$8 per square foot installed in the Madera area. Where a project lands in that range depends on foam thickness (driven by insulation goals and Title 24 requirements), the condition and type of the existing roof, how much prep and repair the substrate needs, roof access and staging, and the complexity of penetrations and details. A straightforward warehouse with good access prices near the bottom of the range; a winery roof crowded with equipment curbs, vents, and piping runs higher. Recoating an existing foam roof runs $2–$4 per square foot — that's the renewal cost that makes the lifecycle math work.

How Long a Foam Roof Lasts — and Why It's Often the Last Roof You Buy

The foam itself does not wear out. What weathers is the protective topcoat, sacrificially, under UV. On the standard maintenance cycle, you recoat every 10–20 years depending on coating thickness and exposure; each recoat resets the clock, and the foam underneath keeps performing. That's the fundamental difference from every membrane system, where end-of-life means tear-off, landfill, and a full repurchase. Well-maintained SPF roofs in the Central Valley have been in continuous service for four decades and counting. We cover the maintenance schedule, warranty considerations, and real-world case history in how long does spray foam roofing last.

Our Installation Process, From Drone Survey to Final Coat

Every Madera project starts with the free assessment: we fly a drone survey of the full roof area, pull core samples where the assembly's history is unclear (critical on older buildings that may carry multiple roof layers), and deliver a written bid within 48 hours. On award, the sequence runs: substrate prep — cleaning, drying, removing saturated areas found in the cores, and priming as needed; masking and wind screening to protect adjacent surfaces, vehicles, and equipment (a real consideration at working wineries and packing houses — we plan overspray control around your operations); foam application in passes to the specified thickness, self-flashing every penetration; then the base and top coats of silicone with granules broadcast into the final coat for traction and hail resistance. Most projects finish in days, not weeks, and the roof is watertight behind the spray gun each day — there's no point in the schedule where your building sits open. Full detail is in our installation process overview.

Chowchilla, Oakhurst, and Coarsegold Coverage

Our Madera service area covers the whole county. In Chowchilla, the work runs to ag processing, dairy-support buildings, and metal shops along the 99 and CA-233 — classic SPF-over-metal territory. Up CA-41 in the foothills, Oakhurst and Coarsegold present a different profile: gateway-to-Yosemite commercial buildings, lodges, restaurants, and shops at 2,000+ feet of elevation, where summers still bake but winters bring real cold snaps and occasional snow load on low-slope sections. SPF performs well in the foothill climate — the insulation value works both directions, and the seamless membrane handles freeze-thaw far better than seamed systems. Drive time from our Tulare County shop runs about an hour to Madera proper and somewhat more into the hill country; either way, these are roads our crews run regularly.

We're a family-owned company, not a franchise or a storm-chasing outfit — more than twenty years of our work is on roofs within an hour's drive of our shop, and our reputation lives or dies in the Valley. We hold California contractor license #C-2-1052735, we're BBB Accredited, and we're SPFA members, which keeps our crews aligned with the industry's application standards for thickness, density, and coating coverage. We back our work with industry-leading leak-proof guarantees, and because we're sixty minutes down the 99, service after the sale is a phone call, not a mystery. When we bid your roof, the numbers come from drone imagery and core data on your actual building — never from a satellite photo and a price-per-square guess.

silicone-roof-coating.body_html:
Silicone Roof Coating in Madera: Restore the Roof You Have

Silicone roof coating gives Madera building owners a way to renew an aging flat, foam, or metal roof for $2–$4 per square foot instead of paying replacement money for a tear-off. A high-solids 100% silicone system is applied as a fluid over your existing roof, cures into a seamless white membrane, and resets the roof's weathering surface for another decade or two. For the wineries along the 99 corridor, the processors and warehouses in the Madera Industrial Park, the metal buildings out the county avenues, and the commercial stock up CA-41 in Oakhurst, coating is very often the smartest roof money available — provided the roof underneath still qualifies, which is exactly what our free drone survey and core sampling determine before we quote anything.

Allstate Spray Foam Roofing has been coating and restoring Valley roofs for more than twenty years. We're family-owned, California-licensed (#C-2-1052735), BBB Accredited, and SPFA members, and our crews reach Madera in about an hour up Highway 99 from our Tulare County shop.

What Makes 100% Silicone Different From Other Coatings

Not all roof coatings behave alike, and the difference matters enormously on Valley flat roofs. Silicone is moisture-cure and hydrophobic: it can sit under standing water indefinitely without softening, re-emulsifying, or losing adhesion. Acrylic coatings — the cheaper alternative you'll see quoted — are water-based, and ponded water does to them roughly what it does to latex paint. On a dead-flat Madera warehouse roof where water lingers for days after a winter storm or sits under weeks of tule fog, that distinction decides whether the coating lasts twenty years or fails in three.

Silicone also holds its properties under UV better than any competing chemistry. Madera's solar exposure is severe — the same sun that ripens the AVA's grapes chalks and embrittles lesser coatings. Silicone weathers by very slowly chalking at the surface while staying flexible and adhered, which is why the recoat cycle runs 10–20 years rather than 5–10. The tradeoff is that once a roof is siliconed, future recoats must also be silicone — nothing else sticks to it reliably — which is a one-time decision, not a real drawback, since silicone-over-silicone recoats are the simplest job in roofing.

Which Madera Roofs Qualify for a Silicone Coating

Coating restores a roof; it doesn't resurrect one. The existing roof must be fundamentally sound, dry, and well-adhered. Good candidates across Madera County include: spray foam roofs due for their scheduled recoat; metal roofs with sound panels but leaking fasteners and laps; single-ply (TPO/EPDM) that's aged but not saturated; and built-up or mod-bit roofs with weathered surfaces but dry insulation. Poor candidates: roofs with widespread saturated insulation (coating traps the moisture), membranes that have lost adhesion, or decks with structural problems. This is why we core-sample before quoting — a coating over wet insulation is money thrown away, and we won't sell it. When cores show saturation, the honest fix is targeted removal and repair first, or a move to a full spray polyurethane foam roofing system where the roof warrants it.

Silicone Roof Coating Pros and Cons

We'd rather you hear the tradeoffs from us than discover them later. The honest ledger:

  • Pro — ponding immunity: silicone is the only mainstream coating that shrugs off standing water, which matters on Madera's many dead-flat roofs and through fog season.
  • Pro — cost: at $2–$4 per square foot, restoration runs a fraction of the $4–$8+ of new roofing, with no tear-off, no landfill fees, and no exposure of the building during work.
  • Pro — reflectivity: a bright white surface knocks rooftop temperatures down dramatically in 100°F+ summers, cutting cooling loads and helping with Title 24 cool-roof compliance on qualifying projects.
  • Pro — seamless and self-flashing: fluid application seals fastener heads, seams, and penetration details in one continuous film.
  • Pro — renewable: when it weathers thin in 10–20 years, you clean and recoat. The cycle repeats indefinitely.
  • Con — slick when wet: uncoated silicone is slippery underfoot; we broadcast granules into walkway areas and around equipment on roofs with regular traffic.
  • Con — adhesion is prep-dependent: silicone bonds only to clean, dry, properly primed substrates. Skipped prep is the number-one cause of coating failure — and the reason to hire a contractor who washes, tests, and primes rather than just sprays.
  • Con — commits future recoats to silicone: as above, a one-time chemistry commitment.
  • Con — not a structural fix: coating adds no insulation and no strength. If the roof needs R-value or the deck needs work, coating alone is the wrong tool.

Silicone Roof Coating Cost in Madera

Silicone restoration in the Madera area typically prices at $2–$4 per square foot installed. The drivers: how much cleaning and prep the existing surface needs, how much repair work (wet-area removal, seam reinforcement, fastener treatment) comes first, specified coating thickness in dry mils, roof access, and detail density — a winery roof crowded with vents, curbs, and piping takes more labor per square than an open warehouse. Compare that against $4–$8 per square foot for a new SPF system or the still-higher cost of tear-off and single-ply replacement, and the appeal is obvious wherever the existing roof qualifies. Recoating Foam Roofs: The Scheduled Renewal

If your building already has an SPF roof, silicone recoating is not an option — it's the maintenance the system is designed around. The foam itself doesn't weather; the topcoat does, sacrificially, under the Valley sun. On the standard cycle you recoat every 10–20 years: we clean the surface, repair any foam damage or blisters found in inspection, and spray fresh silicone to specification. The roof's clock resets, and the foam underneath — with its full R-6.5 per inch still working — never needs replacement. Madera-area foam roofs that have kept this schedule are running strong after three and four decades; the lifecycle evidence is laid out in how long does spray foam roofing last. If your foam roof's coating is chalking heavily, showing exposed yellow-brown foam, or pinholing, don't wait — coating a weathered-but-intact foam roof costs $2–$4 per square foot, while letting UV eat into the foam itself adds repair scope.

Metal Roof Coating for Ag Buildings and Wineries

Madera County's metal buildings — equipment shops, barns, hullers, tank rooms, commodity sheds from Chowchilla to the foothills — are prime coating candidates once fastener leaks start. A silicone metal-roof system starts with prep: wash-down, rust treatment, then detail work where the leaks actually originate: every fastener head gets brushed sealant or a purpose-made cap, every panel lap and ridge gets reinforced, penetrations get flashed with coating and fabric. Then the full-field silicone coat goes on, tying the details into one membrane. The white surface also drops summer panel temperatures sharply — on an uninsulated shop that's an immediate comfort difference, and on a winery tank room it trims the load on process cooling. One honest caveat: coating does not insulate. If your metal building also drips condensation during fog season or bakes in summer, the better answer is often foam over the panels — see our spray foam vs TPO comparison for how the full-system options stack up on metal buildings.

Ponding Water: Madera's Flat-Roof Curse, Silicone's Specialty

Much of Madera's commercial stock was built dead-flat or near it, and decades of settling, added equipment, and clogged drains leave shallow ponds standing on many roofs after every storm. Winter makes it worse: rain arrives in Pacific systems, then tule fog keeps evaporation near zero for days, so water that would flash off a summer roof in hours sits for a week in January. Ponded water accelerates every failure mode a roof has — it magnifies UV, breeds algae and debris dams, overloads structure, and probes relentlessly at seams. Silicone is the only coating chemistry rated to sit under that water indefinitely. During our assessment we map ponding zones from drone imagery, and where practical we correct the worst of them — building drainage crickets from foam, clearing and adding drains — before coating, so the restoration fixes causes as well as symptoms.

What the Process Looks Like on Your Building

Every coating project in Madera starts with the free assessment: full drone survey, core samples where the roof's moisture condition is uncertain, and a written bid within 48 hours. The work itself runs: power-wash and cleaning; repairs — saturated material removed and replaced, seams and splits reinforced, fasteners treated; primer where the substrate chemistry requires it; then silicone applied to specified mil thickness, with granules broadcast into walkways and service paths. Coating work is quiet and low-disruption: no tear-off debris, no dumpsters, minimal odor, and your operation keeps running underneath. For working wineries and food facilities we sequence around production schedules and sanitation zones — we've done this around crush season before, and planning beats apology.

Serving Madera, Chowchilla, Oakhurst, and Coarsegold

From our Tulare County shop it's about sixty minutes up the 99 to Madera, with Chowchilla a short hop further and the CA-41 foothill towns — Coarsegold and Oakhurst — within routine range. Foothill roofs get the same silicone logic with a twist: elevation brings colder winters and occasional snow on low-slope sections, and silicone's flexibility through freeze-thaw cycling outperforms brittle aged membranes. Gateway-corridor businesses in Oakhurst — lodges, restaurants, retail serving Yosemite traffic — also benefit from restoration's speed: days on the roof, not weeks, matters when your parking lot is your revenue.

The roof-coating market attracts overpromisers, so here's our standard: we tell you whether your roof qualifies based on cores and imagery, we tell you when coating is the wrong answer, and we put the price in writing within 48 hours. Will silicone coating stop the ponding-water leaks on my flat roof?

Can you coat the metal roof on my shop or winery building?

My foam roof is 15 years old and chalking. Is that an emergency?

Does a white silicone roof actually lower cooling bills in Madera summers?

On refrigerated and wine-storage buildings that translates directly into reduced cooling runtime.

foam-roof-repair.body_html:
Roof Repair in Madera That Starts With the Real Source of the Leak

Roof repair in Madera usually begins the same way: a stain spreads across a ceiling tile, a drip lands on a barrel rack or a pallet of product, and somebody gets sent up a ladder to guess where the water is coming from. On flat and low-slope roofs — which is most of Madera's commercial, ag, and industrial stock — the guess is usually wrong, because water travels. It enters at a failed seam or a backed-out fastener, runs along the deck or under the membrane, and shows up inside the building twenty or forty feet from the actual breach. That's why our repair work starts with diagnosis, not caulk: drone imagery of the whole roof, a physical inspection of the details water actually exploits, and core samples where we need to know what's happening inside the assembly. We're Allstate Spray Foam Roofing — family-owned, 20+ years in the Valley, California license #C-2-1052735, BBB Accredited, SPFA member — and our crews reach Madera in about an hour up CA-99 from our Tulare County shop.

Flat Roof Repair: Where Madera's Commercial Roofs Fail

The failure points on Valley flat roofs are remarkably consistent. Seams and laps open as the membrane ages and the roof cycles through 100°F+ summer days and cold, damp winters — thermal movement works every joint until one gives. Flashings crack where the roof meets walls, curbs, and equipment stands. Pitch pans dry out around penetrations. Drains clog with ag dust, leaf litter, and coating chalk, then back water up over their flashings. And ponding zones — endemic on Madera's dead-flat buildings — quietly magnify every one of those weaknesses, especially in winter when tule fog holds evaporation near zero and a January pond can stand for a week. On built-up roofs we also see alligatored asphalt and open blisters; on single-ply, punctured membrane from foot traffic and dropped tools around HVAC units. Our repairs match the system: reinforced seam work, rebuilt flashings, new drain assemblies, targeted membrane patching — done to manufacturer detail, not smeared with mastic and hope.

Foam Roof Repair: A Specialty We Actually Specialize In

Spray foam roofs are exceptionally repairable — that's one of their core virtues — but they need a contractor who understands the system, and generalist roofers in the Madera area often don't. The foam itself rarely fails. What happens instead: the protective silicone or acrylic topcoat weathers thin past its 10–20-year cycle and UV starts eating the exposed foam; hail or dropped equipment gouges the surface; birds peck at exposed foam edges; or a poor original application left thin spots and pinholes. The repair logic follows the damage. Small punctures and gouges get cleaned, cut back to sound foam, filled with sealant or spot-applied foam, and recoated. Larger damaged areas get scarfed down, re-foamed, and re-coated to blend with the field. And a roof whose whole topcoat is at end of life doesn't need patch repairs — it needs its scheduled recoat, which at $2–$4 per square foot renews the entire surface. If another contractor has told you a foam roof "can't be fixed" or must be torn off, get a second opinion before you spend replacement money — our foam roof repair guide covers what's actually repairable, which is nearly everything.

Leak Repair for Wineries and Food-Grade Facilities

A roof leak means something different when it's over a barrel room, a bottling line, or a food-processing floor. Madera's wine and food operations — the AVA's wineries, the nut processors, the cold-chain warehouses off the 99 — can't tolerate water over product, and they can't always shut down while a roof gets opened up. We plan repair work around that reality: containment and interior protection before any cutting, sequencing by production zone, sanitation-conscious housekeeping on food sites, and scheduling around crush, harvest, and shipping windows. Condensation deserves special mention here, because in fog season it masquerades as a roof leak: warm humid interior air hits a cold uninsulated deck or metal panel and "rains" indoors with no breach anywhere. We diagnose which one you actually have before anyone sells you a repair — the fix for condensation is insulation and vapor control, not patching sound membrane.

Metal Roof Repair on Ag Buildings

Madera County's metal buildings — shops, barns, hullers, equipment sheds from the west-side avenues to Chowchilla — leak in predictable places: fastener heads whose washers have weathered and backed out (multiplied by the thousands across one roof), panel laps opened by thermal cycling, rusted valleys and ridge details, and skylight panels gone brittle. Piecemeal fixes hold for a season; done right, repair means treating fastener fields systematically with brushed sealant or caps, reinforcing laps with coating and fabric, cutting out rust-through, and replacing failed light panels. When a metal roof's leaks are widespread rather than local, the honest math usually favors restoration — a full silicone coating system or spray foam over the panels — rather than an endless series of service calls. We'll show you that math with real numbers, not pressure; the comparison logic is the same one laid out in our spray foam vs TPO guide.

Repair, Recoat, or Replace: The Decision Table

The most valuable thing we bring to a Madera repair call is an honest read on which category your roof is in. Core samples and drone imagery take the guesswork out of it:

Roof ConditionRight AnswerTypical Cost Range
Localized damage; assembly dry and soundTargeted repairHundreds to low thousands, scope-dependent
Surface weathered; insulation dry; leaks starting at detailsRepair details + full restoration coating$2–$4/sq ft
Foam roof at end of topcoat cycle (10–20 yrs)Scheduled silicone recoat$2–$4/sq ft
Widespread saturation, failed adhesion, or structural issuesReplacement — often SPF over prepared deck$4–$8/sq ft for new SPF

Roughly a third of the "replacement" bids we're asked to check against turn out to be restoration or repair candidates. Cores don't lie, and we put what they show in writing.

Ponding Water Repairs: Fixing the Cause

Standing water is the background condition behind a huge share of Madera flat-roof failures, and patching a leak inside a pond without addressing the pond is a short-term transaction. Where drainage is the root cause we correct it as part of the repair: sculpted foam crickets that re-slope water toward drains, cleared and rebuilt drain bowls, added scuppers or drains where the original design was inadequate, and — on foam roofs — re-foamed low spots that restore positive slope. This is an area where SPF as a material gives us options flat-membrane contractors don't have: foam can be built up in place to any contour, so drainage corrections that would be major carpentry on other systems are spray work on ours. Details on how slope-building fits a full system are in our installation process overview.

When the Roof Is Leaking Right Now

We'll be straight with you about response times rather than invent guarantees: our crews dispatch from our Tulare County shop, about sixty minutes south of Madera on CA-99, and we prioritize active-leak calls — water over product, occupied space, or equipment moves to the front of the schedule. When you call (559) 739-9519 with an active leak, tell us what's under the leak and what kind of roof you have; we'll tell you honestly when we can be there and walk you through immediate containment in the meantime: catch and divert water, move or cover what's below, and if it's safe and accessible, clear the nearest roof drain — a backed-up drain sheeting water over a flashing is one of the most common "sudden" leaks in Madera's winter storm-then-fog pattern. What we won't do is promise a 24/7 fleet we don't operate. We'd rather earn the second call by being honest on the first one.

Storm, Wind, and Hail Damage

The Madera area's storm profile is Pacific fronts with gusty winds, occasional convective cells with small hail, and wind-borne debris — plus the odd surprise off the foothills toward Coarsegold and Oakhurst, where elevation adds snow-load stress and sharper freeze-thaw to low-slope roofs. After a storm, the damage we find most is at the details: lifted flashings and edge metal, membrane punctures from debris, cracked coating at hail impact points, and displaced equipment that's torn its curb flashing. If you're documenting damage for an insurance conversation, our drone survey produces dated, high-resolution imagery of the entire roof surface — useful evidence whether or not you end up filing. We repair what's actually damaged and tell you plainly when a roof's post-storm problems are really pre-storm age.

Repair Costs in Madera, Honestly Framed

Repair pricing depends on scope in a way per-square-foot numbers can't capture, so treat anyone quoting sight-unseen with suspicion. What we can tell you: assessment is free — drone survey, core samples where warranted, written findings and bid within 48 hours. Targeted repairs on an otherwise sound roof typically run in the hundreds to low thousands. Full restoration coating, when the roof qualifies, runs $2–$4 per square foot. Replacement with new spray foam runs $4–$8 per square foot. Where repairs will only buy a season or two, we say so and show you the numbers side by side — the spray foam roofing cost guide lays out the lifecycle comparison we use.

Serving All of Madera County

Our repair territory covers Madera proper — the Industrial Park, the Avenue 12 and Avenue 17 corridors, downtown and the 145 approaches — plus Chowchilla's ag and processing buildings to the north, and the foothill commercial stock up CA-41 through Coarsegold to Oakhurst. Foothill buildings get the same diagnostic-first approach with elevation factored in: snow-melt cycling, colder nights, and pine debris in drains change the failure patterns, and we've seen enough of both climates to know the difference. Family-owned for 20+ years, licensed (#C-2-1052735), BBB Accredited, SPFA member, and backed by industry-leading leak-proof guarantees on the systems we install. Call (559) 739-9519 — the survey is free, the bid takes 48 hours, and the diagnosis is honest either way.
faqs: Who repairs foam roofs in Madera? Most roofers I've called won't touch it.

Foam roofs are actually among the most repairable systems: punctures get cut back and filled, damaged areas get re-foamed, and weathered topcoats get recoated. We've specialized in spray foam systems for over 20 years and repair them routinely across Madera County.
My ceiling is leaking but I can't find any damage on the roof. Why?

On flat roofs, water travels — it enters at a seam, fastener, or flashing and runs along the deck before dripping inside, often dozens of feet from the breach. In fog season it may not even be a leak: condensation on a cold, uninsulated deck mimics one. Our drone survey and physical inspection trace the real source before anything gets patched.
Do you offer emergency roof repair in Madera?

We prioritize active-leak calls — water over product or occupied space moves to the front of our schedule — and we're honest about timing: crews dispatch from our Tulare County shop, about an hour south of Madera. Call (559) 739-9519, tell us what's leaking and what's under it, and we'll give you a real arrival window plus immediate containment steps.
Is it worth repairing my flat roof, or should I just replace it?

Core samples answer that question honestly. If the insulation is dry and damage is localized, repair is the right money. If the surface is aged but the assembly is dry, restoration coating at $2–$4 per square foot beats replacement. Only widespread saturation or structural problems justify replacement cost. We put the findings and both prices in writing within 48 hours.
Water ponds on my Madera warehouse roof every winter. Can that be fixed?

Yes — and it should be, because ponding accelerates every other failure. We build foam crickets to re-slope water toward drains, rebuild clogged or undersized drain assemblies, and on foam roofs re-foam low spots to restore positive slope. Fixing the drainage as part of the repair is what makes the repair last.
Do you handle roof repairs up in Oakhurst and Coarsegold?

We do. The CA-41 foothill corridor is part of our regular Madera County territory. Foothill roofs fail differently — freeze-thaw cycling, snow-melt, pine debris in drains — and we factor elevation into both diagnosis and repair. Drive time from our shop is a bit over an hour, and the free assessment works the same: drone survey, cores if needed, written bid in 48 hours.

commercial-insulation.body_html:
Commercial Spray Foam Insulation for Madera's Working Buildings

Commercial spray foam insulation solves the problem most Madera buildings were born with: they were built to hold equipment, product, and crop — not to hold a temperature. The county's metal shops, warehouses, hullers, packing sheds, winery buildings, and cold-storage boxes overwhelmingly went up as bare or minimally insulated shells, and in Climate Zone 13 that bill comes due twice a year. Summer drives interior temperatures brutal enough to punish workers, equipment, and stored product; winter's tule fog turns every cold metal panel into a condensation machine that literally rains on whatever's below. Closed-cell spray polyurethane foam — applied to roof decks, metal panels, and walls at roughly R-6.5 per inch — fixes both at once, and it's the commercial insulation work we've been doing across the Valley for more than twenty years. To be clear about our lane: we insulate commercial, agricultural, and industrial buildings. We don't do residential work — if you need a house insulated, we're not your contractor, and we'll say so on the phone.

Why Closed-Cell Foam Beats Everything Else in a Metal Building

Closed-cell SPF is the highest-performing insulation you can put in a commercial building, and in a metal building it's arguably the only one that fully works. Its R-6.5 per inch leads every common alternative, so it delivers code-level performance in inches where batt systems need feet. It adheres directly to steel panels and purlins, conforming to every rib and lap with no gaps, no sag, and no fastener penetrations — compare that with vinyl-faced metal-building blanket, which crushes to near-zero R-value at every purlin it crosses and tears at every point a forklift or a repair ever touches it. Closed-cell foam is also a Class II vapor retarder and an air barrier in one material, which is what actually stops fog-season condensation (more below). And it adds rigidity: foam bonded across panels stiffens the whole diaphragm, quieting rattle and oil-canning in wind. Open-cell foam, at roughly half the R-value per inch and vapor-open, has interior uses but is the wrong tool against metal skin in this climate; closed-cell is what we spec for Madera's building stock.

Condensation: The Tule Fog Problem, Solved at the Panel

Ask anyone who runs a metal building between Madera and Chowchilla what January is like inside, and you'll hear about the drip. The physics is simple: fog-season air is saturated, nights are cold, and an uninsulated steel panel sits at outdoor temperature. Warm, moist interior air — from propane heaters, equipment, stored crop respiration, or just people working — touches that cold steel and condenses instantly. The result is water dripping from every purlin line onto equipment, hay, packaged nuts, cased wine, stored machinery. Rust follows on the building; mold and spoilage follow on the contents. Closed-cell foam ends it by breaking the thermal path: with even an inch or two bonded to the panel, the surface the interior air touches is warm foam, not cold steel, and it never reaches dew point. Because the foam is its own vapor retarder and air barrier, humid air can't sneak behind it to find cold metal either — the failure mode that dooms blanket-and-liner retrofits. Condensation control alone justifies foam in a large share of the ag buildings we insulate in Madera County.

Wineries and Temperature-Stable Storage

Madera's wine industry gives insulation work here a specific character. The AVA's wineries run barrel rooms, case-goods storage, tank rooms, and crush facilities where temperature stability is a quality variable, not just a utility line item. Wine in barrel wants steady conditions; every degree of daily swing works the wine and the cooperage. Tank rooms carry process cooling whose runtime tracks the building envelope directly. Closed-cell foam on the roof deck and walls of these buildings flattens the daily temperature curve dramatically — the difference between a metal-skinned barrel barn that tracks the outdoor swing from 105°F afternoons to 65°F nights and one that drifts a few degrees around its setpoint. The same performance serves food-grade processors and cold-chain operators: hullers and processors protecting product condition, refrigerated and freezer storage where every point of R-value is compressor runtime you stop paying for. Foam's seamless application also suits washdown-adjacent spaces — no fibrous insulation to shed, sag, or harbor moisture above a sanitation zone, and interior applications can be finished with coatings where a cleanable surface is required.

Warehouses, the Industrial Park, and Madera's Logistics Growth

Madera's industrial base is expanding as logistics spillover from Fresno pushes north up the 99 — the Madera Industrial Park, the Avenue 12 and Avenue 17 corridors, and new light-industrial development around the city are adding and re-purposing big-box space steadily. For warehouse operators, insulation math is simple and large: an uninsulated or under-insulated roof deck over hundreds of thousands of cubic feet means conditioning costs that scale with every 100°F+ day, and worker-comfort problems that OSHA heat rules have made harder to ignore. Spray foam applied to the underside of the roof deck — or as a spray polyurethane foam roofing system on top, insulating and waterproofing in one move — brings these shells up to modern performance without reconstruction. Title 24 matters here too: California's energy code sets real insulation and envelope requirements when buildings are altered, expanded, or newly conditioned, and foam's per-inch efficiency is often the most practical path to compliance in a retrofit where framing depth is fixed.

Spray Foam vs Fiberglass and Rigid Board: The Honest Comparison

PropertyClosed-Cell SPFFiberglass Batt / BlanketRigid Board (Poly-iso)
R-value per inch~R-6.5~R-3.0–3.7 (less when compressed)~R-5.6–6.0
Air barrierYes — monolithicNoOnly if joints sealed perfectly
Vapor retarderYes (Class II at 1.5"+)Facing only, tears easilyFacer-dependent
Fits metal-building geometryConforms to ribs, laps, purlinsCompressed at every purlinPoor — flat stock on ribbed panels
Condensation control on steelExcellent — bonds to panelPoor — air reaches cold metalFair — gaps defeat it
Adds structural rigidityYesNoNo
Installed costHighest upfrontLowest upfrontMiddle

The pattern: fiberglass is cheap to install and routinely fails to perform in metal buildings; rigid board performs on paper and leaks air at every joint in practice; closed-cell foam costs more per inch and is the only one of the three that delivers its rated performance on a ribbed steel panel in a foggy Valley winter. We'd rather you spend once.

What Commercial Spray Foam Costs in Madera

Interior commercial foam work is priced per square foot at a given thickness, and honest context beats a teaser number. Closed-cell spray foam insulation generally runs in the low single dollars per square foot per inch of thickness for commercial-scale work, with total cost driven by area, specified R-value, surface prep (rust, dust, and oils must be addressed for adhesion), access and lift requirements, masking scope, and whether an ignition-barrier or thermal-barrier coating is required over the foam for code in the space. A large open warehouse deck prices efficiently; a working winery with equipment to protect and zones to sequence takes more labor per square foot. Every job gets the same process: free on-site assessment, and a written bid within 48 hours with thickness, R-value, coatings, and prep spelled out. If the roof itself is also at end of life, ask us to price the rooftop-SPF alternative at the same time — the combined roof-plus-insulation economics, covered in our cost guide, frequently beat doing the two jobs separately.

Roof-Deck Foam vs Rooftop Foam: Two Ways to Insulate, One Assessment

Madera building owners often don't realize they have two spray foam paths to an insulated building. Interior application — foam sprayed to the underside of the roof deck and to wall panels — is the classic insulation retrofit, right when the roof surface itself is sound. Rooftop application — SPF installed over the existing roof as a roofing system — insulates and waterproofs simultaneously, and it's usually the smarter buy when the roof is within a few years of needing work anyway, since $4–$8 per square foot delivers a new seamless roof and R-6.5 per inch in one project. The rooftop system's longevity story — a renewable topcoat on a 10–20-year recoat cycle instead of tear-off — is laid out in how long spray foam roofing lasts. Our assessment looks at both and gives you both numbers when both make sense; the building's condition, not our preference, picks the winner.

Installation With Your Operation Running

Commercial insulation work in an operating facility is a logistics job as much as a spray job, and twenty-plus years of Valley ag and industrial sites have taught us to plan it that way. We mask and shield equipment, racking, and product zones; we sequence work bay by bay so your operation keeps moving; we ventilate per SPFA practice and keep re-entry timing clear so there's no ambiguity about when spaces are back in service; and on food-grade and winery sites we coordinate with your sanitation and QA requirements before the rig shows up. Where code requires an ignition or thermal barrier over interior foam, we include and apply it — an unprotected-foam shortcut is the kind of thing that surfaces at your next fire inspection, and we don't take it. Most metal-building and warehouse projects run days, not weeks.

Serving Madera, Chowchilla, Oakhurst, and Coarsegold

From our Tulare County shop, Madera is about sixty minutes north on CA-99 — routine territory, along with Chowchilla's dairy-support and processing buildings, the west-side ranch shops off CA-145, and the CA-41 foothill corridor through Coarsegold up to Oakhurst. The foothill towns flip the insulation problem seasonally: gateway-to-Yosemite businesses and shop buildings at elevation see real winter cold along with summer heat, and closed-cell foam serves both directions of that swing. Wherever the building is, the process is the same: free assessment, core data and measurements where needed, and a written bid within 48 hours from a family-owned contractor — license #C-2-1052735, BBB Accredited, SPFA member. Call (559) 739-9519 and tell us what the building does; we'll insulate it for that job.
faqs: Do you insulate residential homes in Madera?

No — commercial, agricultural, and industrial buildings only. Metal shops, warehouses, wineries, processing plants, and cold storage are our lane. If you call about a house we'll tell you straight and save you the site visit; for a commercial building anywhere in Madera County, the assessment is free.
Will spray foam stop the winter condensation dripping inside my metal building?

Yes — this is one of the most common reasons Madera ag buildings call us. Closed-cell foam bonded to the panels keeps the interior surface warm enough that fog-season air can never reach dew point on it, and because the foam is its own air and vapor barrier, humid air can't get behind it to find cold steel. The drip stops.
How much R-value do I need for a warehouse or winery building in Madera?

Climate Zone 13's heat drives the answer, and Title 24 sets minimums when a building is altered or newly conditioned. Closed-cell foam delivers about R-6.5 per inch, so typical roof-deck applications of two to three inches land in the R-13 to R-20 range. We specify exact thickness in your written bid based on the building, its use, and applicable code.
Is spray foam worth the extra cost over fiberglass in a metal building?

In a metal building, usually yes — and often it's the only option that actually performs. Metal-building blanket compresses to near-zero R-value at every purlin and tears easily, and fiberglass does nothing to stop air from reaching cold panels, so condensation continues. Closed-cell foam conforms to the panel geometry, air-seals, vapor-retards, and stiffens the structure in one application.
Can you insulate our winery without shutting down production?

In most cases yes. We sequence work zone by zone, mask and protect tanks, barrels, and equipment, ventilate per SPFA practice with clear re-entry timing, and coordinate scheduling around crush, bottling, and sanitation requirements. Madera-area wineries and food facilities are a regular part of our work, and the planning happens before the spray rig arrives.
Should I insulate under my roof deck or put foam on top of the roof instead?

It depends on the roof's condition. If the roof surface is sound, interior foam under the deck is the straightforward retrofit. If the roof is also near end of life, rooftop SPF at $4–$8 per square foot waterproofs and insulates in one project and is often the better total spend. Our free assessment prices both paths when both apply.
